passages.text: <!-- vale ai-tells.ExplainerHeadings = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The subject is neuroscience: how groups of nerve cells represent information used in memory, eye control, and navigation. The three papers examine mathematical models that store a quantity such as an angle, eye movements and neural activity recorded in macaque monkeys, and location-dependent neural activity recorded in rodents and bats. [They ask how activity can retain a value, how an internal fluctuation can move the eyes, and why a cell can respond at several separate locations.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = NO --> A remembered direction must remain useful after its cue disappears. The eyes must hold an angle while an animal looks at a target. A moving animal must keep track of where it is. These tasks depend on groups of [[**neuron**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s, the brain's signaling cells]{.definition-explanation}, whose electrical signals are brief and variable. Computational and systems neuroscience studies how these cells and their interactions support such behavior. Mathematical models connect assumptions about cells and their interactions to predictions. Recordings test those predictions against neural activity and movement. <!-- vale ai-tells.BareHolds = YES -->

Burak and Fiete (2012) study short-term memory for a continuous quantity, such as a direction or eye angle. A proposed mechanism is that interacting neurons keep activity going after the original input ends. [Yet the remembered value can change while the activity persists.]{.key-statement} The problem is to explain how the properties of the cells and their connections set the rate of this loss of accuracy.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The authors analyze a network with a continuous family of persistent activity patterns, each representing a different value. Each cell sends signals at random times. They use an approximation for small fluctuations to derive how these signals move the stored value, compare the calculation with network simulations, and relate the motion to the best accuracy possible when estimating the stored value from those signals. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> [Their central result is a lower bound: the uncertainty in reading the network's current value limits how slowly that value can wander.]{.key-statement} Under the model's assumptions, the variance of the memory error grows with storage time. Reading for longer also has diminishing benefit because the state continues moving during observation. This gives a benchmark for evaluating proposed memory circuits and their recall errors. It applies to the analyzed family of continuous-state memory models, with the required noise assumptions and no external signal anchoring the value. Chapters 3–6 develop the [diffusion calculation](../chapters/ch-memory-dynamics.html), its long-delay behavior, the [information bound](../chapters/ch-memory-information.html), and the limits of [readout](../chapters/ch-memory-readout.html).[^orientation-memory] <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> [Even while gaze is held on a stationary target, the eyes move smoothly and irregularly between brief, rapid movements. This smooth motion is called [**fixational drift**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} It changes the image reaching the [[**retina**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, the light-sensitive tissue at the back of the eye]{.definition-explanation}. Understanding its source is therefore part of understanding the visual signals the brain receives. [Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022) ask whether the motion begins mainly in muscles or in neural commands sent to them.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.BareReaches = YES -->

They reanalyze recordings from 57 neurons that send commands to eye muscles in two macaques, paired with precise eye-position measurements. They first calibrate the relation between each cell's activity and larger eye movements. They then use it during fixation to compare the movement predicted from one cell with the measured movement. A separate circuit model tests whether a wandering stored eye-position command could explain the movement's amplitude and time dependence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> For 350-millisecond intervals, their analysis estimates that about 82% of horizontal displacement variance comes from a common source before the final motor neurons, assuming the fitted movement relation also holds during fixation and the relevant noise contributions do not vary together. This supports a central neural contribution to drift. The memory-circuit model provides a possible explanation of that contribution, linking an internal storage error to observable behavior. The recordings do not uniquely locate the noise inside that memory circuit. Chapters 7–9 separate the [shared-drive inference](../chapters/ch-eye-drift.html), the [timing of drift](../chapters/ch-eye-timing.html), and the [proposed circuit mechanism](../chapters/ch-eye-circuit.html).[^orientation-eye] <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> [A [**place cell**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} in the [**hippocampus**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a brain region involved in memory and navigation, becomes more active in particular locations.]{.definition-explanation} [Each connected region of elevated activity is a [**place field**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Small environments encouraged a picture of one smooth field per cell. Larger environments reveal multiple fields with widely varying sizes and shapes. [Mainali, Azeredo da Silveira, and Burak (2025) ask whether one statistical account can explain this variety across species and spatial dimensions.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPaddingStacked = YES -->

Their model gives each cell a smooth random function of location and allows activity where that function exceeds a threshold. The authors derive predictions for the resulting regions, simulate the model, and compare it with existing rodent and bat recordings from one-, two- and three-dimensional environments. Parameters fitted to field sizes and their spatial arrangement also support further tests of field shapes and connectedness.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> The model explains different size distributions across dimensions and predicts additional features, such as multiple peaks within a field and inactive holes surrounded by activity. This makes irregular spatial responses quantitatively understandable and supports a common statistical description across the examined settings. Such statistics can arise when cells combine many inputs through largely random connections. The study does not directly measure those connections. Chapters 10–12 develop the [spatial model](../chapters/ch-place-fields.html), its [size and shape predictions](../chapters/ch-place-sizes.html), and the [tests and circuit interpretation](../chapters/ch-place-tests.html). They distinguish exact predictions, limiting approximations and empirical comparisons.[^orientation-place] <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The three contributions therefore have different meanings: a mathematical constraint on memory models, evidence about the source of eye movement, and a statistical explanation of spatial activity. Together they show how a representation can be described, maintained and related to behavior. Combining all three in one biological circuit remains a further research question, developed in [Chapter 13](../chapters/ch-synthesis.html). <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.ServesAsDodge = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> [Part III](../parts/part-hardware.html) asks how the neural memory mechanisms can be implemented in electronic circuits. The setting is neuromorphic computing, where engineered systems implement computations inspired by neural organization and dynamics. The chapters distinguish connection weights from changing neural states, explain how feedback affects retention, and examine selected hardware research through October 30, 2026. They end with a proposed experiment that separates systematic drift, random spreading, and readout error. This extension is a comparison of mechanisms and evidence. The original papers remain the foundation of Parts I and II. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

[Part IV](../parts/part-simulations.html) follows the computational methods in Burak and Fiete (2012), Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), and Mainali et al. (2025). It distinguishes simulated neural trajectories, recorded-data analysis, and generated spatial maps. Each chapter identifies the model states, numerical procedure, measurements, available code, and limits on reproducing the published figures. The final chapter compares tools and explains resolution and repeatability checks. These are explanations of the sources, not a claim that the guide reran their full simulations.

Part introductions identify the paper behind each chapter's result using author and year. **Central** marks a main finding of that paper. **Supporting** marks an analysis used to establish or qualify it. **Background** supplies needed concepts. **Guide-derived** marks expanded explanations, comparisons, or proposed tests developed here. A result can be central in its own paper while serving as supporting evidence in another argument.

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO --> The guide assumes undergraduate calculus, basic probability, and linear algebra. Neuroscience terms and the required stochastic-process, information, filtering, and random-field ideas are taught where needed. The reading path builds from the signals to the models and then their tests: <!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->

**Chapters 1–2:** establish [neural signals and variability](../chapters/ch-foundations.html), then [persistence and accumulated error](../chapters/ch-persistence.html). <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->

**Chapters 3–6:** derive memory diffusion, its long-delay behavior, the information bound, and readout. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
**Chapters 7–9:** follow the eye study from shared-drive evidence through timing to a circuit model. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
**Chapters 10–12:** develop spatial maps, their size predictions, and tests of their shapes and possible origins. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
**Chapter 13:** connect the results and compare related work.
<!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = NO --> For a path focused on particular papers: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmptyPadding = YES -->
**Memory and eye drift:** follow chapters 1 through 9 in order. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO -->
**Place fields:** read the two foundations chapters and then chapters 10–12. The spatial calculation does not require the readout derivation in chapter 6. <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->

The Glossary gives short definitions for lookup after their first explanation. The References section gives full source details. The original paper figures are discussed by number and can be inspected in the linked PDFs.
After the foundations, the [guide map](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#fig-foundations-paper-map) shows the three paper questions together.

On a first reading, follow the main text, figures, assumptions, and results. The expandable notes preserve longer calculations and extensions. Open one when you want to check the steps behind a result. The explanations needed for the next section remain in the main text.

<!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = NO --> Chapters 3–6 explain [how interacting neurons can retain a value while random spike timing changes it.]{.key-statement} Their treatment of the Burak and Fiete appendix separates three parts of each substantial topic: <!-- vale ai-tells.EmDashUsage = YES -->
<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->

**Neural mechanism:** which cells and signals interact, what changes, and which features are assumptions of the model. For readout, this part also states what an observer can measure and which value it must estimate. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO -->
**Mathematical derivation:** the general tool, its conditions, and the calculation after neural quantities are assigned to the symbols. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->
**Interpretation:** what the result predicts about memory or readout, and what its assumptions leave unresolved.

<!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = NO --> [An equation that specifies how a cell responds belongs to the model. A derivation works out what follows from that choice.]{.key-statement} <!-- vale ai-tells.StackedAnaphora = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = NO --> For example, a spike can disturb several cells' activity. The circuit's interactions remove some changes, while others leave the represented angle displaced. Linear algebra calculates which part survives. Probability gives the spread of that displacement. The result then predicts how quickly memory errors accumulate in this model. The mathematical tools also apply to other systems, but this neural prediction depends on the circuit and spike statistics used in the calculation. <!-- vale ai-tells.FormalTransitions = YES -->

The same distinction matters for readout. A calculation of the best possible estimate sets a benchmark under specified access to neural signals. Establishing that an animal's neurons implement the assumed computation requires separate evidence.

<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = NO --> For a first conceptual pass, read the mechanism, inspect the displayed result and its variables, then read the interpretation. Follow the mathematical derivation when you want to understand why the result holds or calculate with it. Assumptions remain part of both readings. <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeHolds = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO --> The [PNAS appendix](https://www.pnas.org/action/downloadSupplement?doi=10.1073%2Fpnas.1117386109&file=Appendix.pdf) supplies both neural-model choices and mathematical arguments. This map links its seven sections to the guide's explanations. Page links open the local copy. The guide sometimes uses an equivalent teaching derivation and identifies source inconsistencies beside the affected calculation. <!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = NO --> Examples chosen for the guide distinguish independent from shared fluctuations, complete from limited access to neural signals, and exact formulas from approximations for rare fields. Their numbers are checked separately from the published experimental measurements. A teaching reconstruction is labeled when its simplified model differs from the paper's full model. <!-- vale ai-tells.AnthropomorphicCognition = YES -->

<!-- vale ai-tells.RestatementMarkers = NO --> The guide explains how to interpret the experiments and their figures. It does not rerun the original animal recordings, data processing, or full neural-network simulations. [A successful numerical check of a probability identity is different from an independent reproduction of a paper's empirical result.]{.key-statement} Related work is selected to clarify the assumptions and alternatives rather than to claim an exhaustive literature search. <!-- vale ai-tells.RestatementMarkers = YES -->

Throughout the guide, $D$ denotes the [[**diffusion coefficient**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, which sets how quickly uncertainty spreads]{.definition-explanation}. In the basic one-dimensional model, $D$ is constant, neither direction is favored, and no boundary limits the motion. Its [[**mean squared displacement**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} (MSD), the average squared change in the represented coordinate after elapsed time $t$]{.definition-explanation}, is $2Dt$. [Chapter 2](../chapters/ch-persistence.html#sec-foundations-diffusion) explains this model and its assumptions.
The other recurring symbols are:
$d$: spatial dimension.
$\theta$: the represented coordinate in the memory chapters.
$q$: the normalized threshold in the place-field chapters, called $\theta$ in that paper.
$C$: the spatial covariance in the place-field chapters.
The copies are the published versions. Supporting information is linked separately.

<!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = NO --> <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The eyes can hold a position after a brief movement command has ended. An animal can also keep track of its location while the activity of individual neurons fluctuates. [Both abilities require a useful quantity to remain represented in a changing biological system.]{.key-statement} The three papers study different parts of this problem: the loss of a stored value, the origin of slow eye motion, and the arrangement of spatial firing patterns. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES --> <!-- vale ai-tells.CataphoricForecasting = YES -->

Before asking how a circuit keeps a value, we need to know what its signals do. We begin with brief neural spikes and the eye muscles they activate, explaining how repeated activation can maintain an eye angle. We next establish the equations that connect spikes, synaptic input and firing rate. With that physical meaning in place, we ask how a pattern of rates represents an angle or an animal's location. A model of spike counts shows why one brief observation can be uncertain and how combining counts from several cells can help. Finally, we separate shared variation, random spreading and a change in the average value. These distinctions prepare us to interpret both a memory model and measurements of eye motion.
For the eye to stay directed at a target, its muscles must keep exerting force after the movement command ends.

<!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = NO --> [A neuron communicates through brief electrical events called [**spike**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}s.]{.definition-explanation} [A [**firing rate**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is the expected number of spikes per unit time.]{.definition-explanation} A rate of 20 hertz means an average of 20 spikes per second under the specified conditions, rather than a promise of one spike every 50 milliseconds. <!-- vale ai-tells.StrawmanContrast = YES -->

**Anatomy: muscles turn the eyeball.** In humans and macaques, the eyeball rotates within the bony eye socket, or orbit. [The six [**extraocular muscles**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} attach to the outside of the eyeball and control its orientation.]{.definition-explanation} The medial rectus pulls it toward the nose; the lateral rectus pulls it away. The superior and inferior rectus and the two oblique muscles contribute to vertical movement and rotation about the line of sight. Their actions depend on the eye's orientation.[^p-eye-anatomy]

[**Ocular motoneurons (OMNs)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [are neurons that activate these muscles through long nerve fibres.]{.definition-explanation} Their cell bodies lie in brainstem groups, and these fibres travel through three cranial nerves. The abducens nerve, VI, supplies the lateral rectus; the trochlear nerve, IV, supplies the superior oblique; the oculomotor nerve, III, supplies the other four. For horizontal gaze, changing the relative pull of the medial and lateral rectus rotates the eye. [A force's turning effect is its [**torque**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}.]{.definition-explanation} Opposing torques can balance even while the muscles remain under tension.[^p-eye-anatomy]

**Repeated spikes maintain tension.** Each motor spike affects muscle force for longer than the electrical event lasts. Repeated activation and the combined action of many muscle fibres give a smoother force than a sequence of isolated eye movements. [**Tonic firing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [means sustained firing during the holding period.]{.definition-explanation} It need not be perfectly periodic. During a rapid repositioning movement, called a [**saccade**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, a brief strong drive moves the eye; a sustained position-dependent drive then holds the new angle. This is the pulse-and-step description: the step means continuing drive, not one more spike.[^p-eye-mechanics][^p-eye-plasticity]
The mechanical properties contribute in different ways:

[**Elasticity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [creates restoring forces when muscles and surrounding tissues are stretched.]{.definition-explanation} At an off-centre gaze angle, active muscle torque must balance the restoring tendency.

[**Viscosity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [resists motion and dissipates mechanical energy.]{.definition-explanation} It damps rapid changes but supplies no holding torque once velocity is zero.

[**Inertia**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [is resistance to a change in angular velocity.]{.definition-explanation} It matters during acceleration, not as a force holding a stationary eye. In primate eye movements, elastic and viscous effects dominate inertia.[^p-eye-mechanics]

[Mechanical damping smooths movement; sustained neural drive selects the angle around which the eye is held. Inertia cannot preserve a stationary gaze against an unbalanced elastic pull.]{.key-statement}
So far we have followed the output from motor neurons to muscles. The next step is a model of how neurons act on one another and sustain a signal.

**Neural mechanism.** How can brief spikes maintain a state for much longer than the duration of a spike? In this model, each spike leaves a synaptic activation that decays gradually. Holding the eye at an angle requires muscles to maintain tension after the command to move has ended. The brain must therefore keep producing a position-dependent signal. The horizontal eye angle considered here is one number, but a circuit can represent it through thousands of neural activities. A disturbance can change those activities without changing the represented value. Another disturbance can leave a coherent activity pattern while changing the value. The geometry of these two changes will explain why a stable-looking circuit can still accumulate memory error.[^f-memory]

<!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = NO --> Chapter 1 established how spikes act on eye muscles and how firing rates can represent an angle. We now examine the mechanical balance and continuing neural command needed to hold that angle. A small circuit example then shows why some disturbances fade while others leave a different stored angle. Repeating those lasting changes gives the diffusion calculation. The final distinction is between this changing value and an irregular spatial map that stays fixed. It explains why the memory, eye-motion, and place-field papers need different models even though all three concern variable neural signals. <!-- vale ai-tells.FigurativeStays = YES -->

We now separate two questions: how that force balances the eye's elastic pull, and how the brain maintains the command that produces it. The folded calculation answers the mechanical question; the experiments below test the neural one.

**The brain maintains the holding command.** [The [**oculomotor integrator**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} converts movement commands into a maintained eye-position signal.]{.definition-explanation} This signal sustains the motor output after a saccade. The name refers to accumulating an eye-velocity command over time into a position signal. In monkeys, Cannon and Robinson (1987) reversibly disrupted brainstem regions involved in this function. Horizontal gaze then drifted back with a time constant of about 0.2 s, compared with more than 20 s before disruption in darkness. The muscles alone did not provide the original persistence.[^p-eye-integrator]

Visual feedback can correct gaze errors, and signals from the inner ear help compensate for head motion. Holding can nevertheless continue in darkness, so immediate visual correction is not the whole mechanism. [**Plasticity**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} [is a lasting, experience-dependent change in neural responses or connections.]{.definition-explanation} It can adjust how well the holding circuit is calibrated. Major et al. (2004) altered visual feedback in goldfish and trained their gaze holding toward drift or instability over tens of minutes to hours; normal feedback could reverse the change. That is a change in neural control over a longer timescale, distinct from the immediate elastic and viscous response of the tissues. The experiment did not identify the exact cellular learning rule.[^p-eye-anatomy][^p-eye-plasticity]

For a circuit representing position, three questions arise:
**Spatial map:** What activity pattern corresponds to each position? The place-field model addresses this question.
**Memory motion:** How does the represented position evolve when there is no corrective input? The persistent-activity model addresses this question.

**Observed movement:** How does a downstream physical system transform that changing signal into an observable movement? The eye-drift model combines a candidate account of memory motion with a detailed account of this transformation.[^s-three]

The objects differ even when the word position appears in all three. In 2012, $\theta(t)$ locates a network state on its attractor. In 2022, the internal eye-position command and actual eye angle are separate quantities linked through motor neurons and mechanics. In 2025, $x$ locates an animal in an environment, and $h_i(x)$ is a spatial input function assigned to a cell. The Gaussian process does not update a remembered $x$ through time.

A silicon circuit can keep a connection strength unchanged while losing the angle it was asked to remember. It can also keep that angle while its individual electrical signals change. To compare electronic memory with the neural memory in Part I, we first need to identify what information each physical quantity represents. This chapter separates the connection settings, the changing state of each artificial neuron, and the value represented by their joint activity. That separation will let us ask what feedback actually preserves.

Imagine giving a circuit a brief cue for an angle of $30^\circ$. After the cue ends, a connected group of artificial neurons remains active. We estimate the remembered angle from which neurons are active and how strongly. The experiment involves:
**Connection weights** determine how a signal from one neuron changes another neuron's state. A weight can be fixed throughout the trial.
**Neuron and synapse states** change during the trial. Examples include a voltage, a current left by recent inputs, or a number representing either quantity.
**The remembered angle** is a property of the joint state, recovered by a readout rule. It need not occupy one dedicated storage cell.

[Keeping the weights unchanged preserves the circuit's rule of operation. Keeping the cue available requires the resulting activity to preserve information about that cue.]{.key-statement} Training can change the first object. Remembering a new angle can change the second and third without any further training.

[[**Neuromorphic computing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} implements computations inspired by neural circuits using electronic systems organized around neurons, connections, events, or their dynamics.]{.definition-explanation} Some systems calculate neural states as digital numbers. Others use voltages and currents that evolve physically. A system can combine both approaches. The word alone does not tell us where its memory is stored or whether it demonstrates a biological memory mechanism.

[[**Working memory**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, in this Part, means keeping information about a recent input available for a later task.]{.definition-explanation} Persistent activity is one candidate mechanism. A slowly decaying state, a sequence of states, or an explicit digital buffer can also store recent information. We must specify the allowed delay and readout error before calling one implementation adequate.
<div class="publisher-worked-calculation publisher-fold-always">
**Example: the same weights can hold different angles.**

Suppose a ring of 32 artificial neurons has fixed local excitation and broader inhibition. A cue near neuron 3 creates a localized group of active neurons there. A later trial cues neuron 11 and creates a group near that location. The same connection weights support both trials. A decoder assigns an angle to the active group's center. If the group moves after the cue, the decoded angle changes even though every stored weight remains correct. This is an example constructed to illustrate the distinction. It is not a specification of a chip.

The neural model still needs a physical implementation. If the model has a variable called membrane voltage, a chip may store it as a binary number or as an actual circuit voltage. Those choices expose the computation to different errors. [[**Current**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is electric charge flowing per unit time, measured in amperes (coulombs per second).]{.definition-explanation} [[**Voltage**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is an electrical energy difference per unit charge, measured in volts (joules per coulomb).]{.definition-explanation}

A [[**capacitor**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} stores separated electric charge. For fixed capacitance $C$, its stored charge $Q$ and voltage difference $V$ satisfy $Q=CV$.]{.definition-explanation} Charge is measured in coulombs and capacitance in farads (coulombs per volt). Supplying current changes $Q$, so it changes the stored voltage.

<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> [[**Digital storage**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} uses distinguishable physical ranges to represent discrete symbols, usually bits.]{.definition-explanation} In [[**static random-access memory (SRAM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, powered transistor feedback maintains one of two states representing a bit.]{.definition-explanation} Several bits can encode a weight or a changing neuron variable. Reliable bits do not imply unlimited numerical precision: a finite word represents only finitely many values. <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->

[[**Analog state**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} represents a model quantity through the magnitude of a physical variable, such as capacitor voltage.]{.definition-explanation} Input current changes stored charge and so changes voltage. Leakage changes that voltage during a quiet interval. Feedback or new input can oppose the leakage. In BrainScaleS-2, the membrane state evolves this way, while local SRAM stores the synaptic weights.[^hardware-pehle]

[[**Phase-change memory (PCM)**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} stores information in a material's atomic arrangement, including the proportions of ordered and disordered regions, which affect its electrical resistance.]{.definition-explanation} Programming pulses heat the material. Its heating and cooling history changes the arrangement. [[**Conductance**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} measures the current produced per unit applied voltage where current is approximately proportional to voltage. It is the inverse of resistance, the voltage required per unit current.]{.definition-explanation} Reading the conductance can recover a stored weight. Such storage is [[**nonvolatile**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: it can retain its state without continuous power, within its retention limits.]{.definition-explanation} Nonvolatile weights can remain after the changing neural state has disappeared.
The following choices locate the stored quantity before we compare complete machines.

Here [[**device mismatch**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} means persistent differences between nominally identical circuit elements.]{.definition-explanation} It differs from fluctuations that vary from moment to moment. A fixed mismatch can create a repeatable bias. Changing noise can create a different trajectory on each trial. We will measure these separately.

To understand a machine's memory, follow one input through it. On a digital spiking processor, an arriving event identifies connections, their weights contribute to inputs, and a program updates stored neuron variables. Those variables determine whether to send further events. Loihi 2 provides local digital state and weight memory with programmable neuron and learning rules. SpiNNaker2 uses many processor cores whose software updates neural states stored with weights in local SRAM. Their event communication does not make every model variable evolve continuously in physical time.[^hardware-intel][^hardware-spinnaker]

In an analog neural circuit, an input can directly supply current to a capacitor. Transistors implement leakage and other responses as the voltage evolves. Digital circuits may still route the events and store the settings. [[**Mixed-signal hardware**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} combines analog circuit variables with digital storage, communication, or calculation.]{.definition-explanation} The division of labor, rather than the label, determines which dynamics are physical and which are calculated.

PCM supplies a third use of physics. At a fixed, sufficiently small read voltage, a cell's current is approximately $I=GV$, where $I$ is current, $V$ is applied voltage, and $G$ is conductance, measured in siemens (amperes per volt). The stored conductance represents a weight. In Le Gallo and colleagues' chip, the duration of a read pulse represents the input magnitude. For one positive contribution with fixed $G$ and $V$, a pulse lasting $T$ seconds passes charge $Q\simeq GVT$. The contribution is proportional to the product of weight and input duration. Currents from several cells add, and the chip converts the combined current over time to digital values. Signed inputs and weights require additional polarity handling beyond this simple example.[^hardware-legallo]

[[**In-memory computing**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} performs some operations where the values are stored, reducing the need to transfer them to a separate arithmetic unit.]{.definition-explanation} The 64-core PCM chip demonstrates this approach to neural-network inference, with digital processing also part of the system. Its weighted response results from both the stored material state and the applied input signal.

[A circuit's storage medium tells us how a value is retained between updates. Its update rule tells us how that value affects subsequent computation. Both are needed to explain memory.]{.key-statement} We can now examine why feedback can preserve a bit yet let a graded estimate wander.

<!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = NO --> A circuit can remain active for seconds even when its individual voltages decay in milliseconds. The explanation is feedback: activity supplies new input before old input disappears. But long-lived activity does not by itself identify what is being preserved. This chapter first explains how feedback extends a time scale, then distinguishes a restoring discrete memory from a freely changing continuous one. Measured silicon circuits show why this distinction matters beyond a mathematical model. <!-- vale ai-tells.ParallelStaccato = YES -->

In a recurrent circuit, its output can cause an input current that replaces some of that charge. The competition between loss and replacement sets the decay of the collective state. For a neural population, the same competition occurs between decay of synaptic input and input supplied by recurrent spikes.

**Physical mechanism.** In a two-state electronic memory, feedback pushes a slightly disturbed state back toward the same stable state. A sufficiently large disturbance can switch it to the other state. In an ideal continuous attractor, disturbances away from the family of memory states decay, but a displacement along that family represents another valid value. The circuit has no restoring signal telling it which earlier value to recover. Seung used this distinction to compare discrete electronic memory with graded eye-position memory.[^dynamics-seung]

<!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = NO --> This is a distinction between dynamics, not a division between all digital and all analog machines. Analog transistors can maintain discrete bits. Digital processors can calculate a continuous-state neural model to finite precision. Stored bits may remain correct while repeated numerical updates produce a wandering decoded angle. <!-- vale ai-tells.ContrastiveFormulas = YES -->

A physical demonstration lets us test whether feedback maintains the intended state despite unequal devices and finite resolution. The following early experiments make different claims and should be read separately.

Massoud and Horiuchi built a head-direction circuit whose localized activity could persist after a cue and move with velocity input. It had 32 bump positions around a circle, a spacing of $11.25^\circ$. This demonstrates a physical orientation representation with finite resolution. It does not establish an exact continuum of persistent states or a measured Brownian diffusion law.[^dynamics-massoud]

Giulioni and colleagues built a recurrent spiking circuit with low and high activity states. Brief stimulation could initiate activity lasting seconds despite millisecond circuit dynamics. Their measurements also examined noise-driven transitions and recovery after disturbance. This is [[**bistability**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}: two locally stable states under the same ongoing conditions.]{.definition-explanation} It supplies a physical working-memory example, but its two-state retention is a different task from retaining an arbitrary angle.[^dynamics-giulioni]

The comparison gives a useful reading rule for current machines: determine what values the network distinguishes, then ask how long and how accurately it preserves them. Neuron count or nonvolatile weight storage cannot answer those questions alone.

Suppose we want to study how a noisy network retains an angle. One machine can calculate every state update as arithmetic. Another can let capacitor voltages perform part of the dynamics. A third can use material conductances to multiply inputs by stored weights. The scientific choice is which physical effects we want to control, measure, or exploit. This chapter compares these implementations and then examines recent demonstrations of memory and learning.

<!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> The research snapshot is **October 30, 2026**. “State of the art” here means selected recent capabilities supported by primary papers, with older architecture papers supplying their physical explanation. It does not mean one machine leads every task. We distinguish measured chips, experiments partly run on a separate computer, and proposed hardware evaluated by simulation. A [[**host computer**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a separate general-purpose computer that controls an experiment or performs calculations assigned outside the neuromorphic chip.]{.definition-explanation} <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

If the question concerns physical circuit variability, analog dynamics expose that variability directly. Interpreting either choice as a biological result requires a matched model and experiment. [[**Hardware calibration**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} adjusts circuit settings to make measured device responses match requested responses more closely.]{.definition-explanation}

The following studies make progress on different parts of the memory problem. For each, ask what information persists and which physical component is responsible.

**A useful input history on Loihi 2, 2025.** Kleyko and colleagues implemented a stored history of recent inputs and functions of those inputs that include products. A trained readout uses these values to predict an output. This shows that changing chip state can supply useful information about recent inputs. It is not a measurement of indefinitely stable cue retention. Their pictured Hala Point system is much larger than the resources used in the experiment.[^systems-kleyko]

**Persistent spatial activity on SpiNNaker 2, September 2026.** Aitsam and colleagues ran a 768-neuron recurrent sheet on one chip, with signals from a physical event camera. During an eight-second interval without input, the decoded activity center moved by at most half a cell. The eight seconds establish persistence for that interval, not a measured lifetime. The robot-guidance evaluation used a simulated robot. Its power figures were estimates. The study supplies a current physical implementation on which longer-delay and noise-controlled tests would be useful.[^systems-aitsam]

**Rapid adaptation using PCM, 2025.** Ortner and colleagues used physical PCM weights for a recurrent spiking network that produced robotic-arm commands after a task-specific update. Earlier training adjusted the model for rapid adaptation to new tasks. The PCM units performed matrix-vector products. Other operations ran on a host computer. **Example: the update interval determines the physical memory time.**

If updates are separated by $\Delta t$, equating $\alpha^n$ with $e^{-n\Delta t/\tau_m}$ gives $\tau_m=-\Delta t/\ln\alpha$. With $\Delta t=1$ ms and $\alpha=0.999$, $\tau_m$ is about 1 second. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = NO --> After a circuit receives an angle cue, its later estimate may be wrong because the state wandered, because unequal connections pull it toward another angle, or because the observer reads it poorly. One accuracy score combines these causes. The controlled tests below connect these errors to physical parameters. The protocol and reduced models below are proposed tools for reasoning about these experiments, not results already demonstrated on every platform in the previous chapter. <!-- vale ai-tells.VerbTricolon = YES -->

Begin with a circuit whose joint activity represents an angle. Choose a decoder on separate calibration data, then keep it fixed while testing retention. A [[**decoder**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a specified rule for estimating the represented quantity from observable circuit signals.]{.definition-explanation} A decoder given every internal state has a different task from a downstream neuron receiving only spikes.
Use the following sequence:
Present a brief cue for angle $\theta_0$, then remove it. Test many angles, including values between any suspected preferred positions.
Hold the connection weights fixed during each retention trial. Record the actual settings, temperature, update interval, and any imposed noise.

Repeat trials at several delays $t$ and decode $\hat\theta(t)$. Use a common reference for angular differences. [[**Unwrapping**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} tracks crossings of $0^\circ/360^\circ$ by adding or subtracting full turns to continue the trajectory.]{.definition-explanation} Use it only when sampling is frequent enough to identify crossings reliably.
Report mean error and error variance separately as functions of cue and delay. Also report failures in which the activity pattern disappears or changes form.
Repeat with changed noise, calibration, or numerical precision, changing one factor at a time. Compare with the same model running in a numerical reference implementation.

Record the decoded state immediately after each cue so that error in writing the value can be separated from error accumulated during retention. Report the number of repeated trials and uncertainty in the estimated drift and diffusion.

[An active circuit has demonstrated useful memory only when its later signals distinguish the earlier cues at the required accuracy.]{.key-statement} High firing rate alone does not establish this. Nor does a small average error if positive and negative errors cancel.
For short intervals, a useful local model is

Here $b(\theta)$ is systematic angular motion per unit time and $D(\theta)$ is half the local variance growth rate. With nearly constant coefficients over a short lag $\Delta t$, repeated trials near the same angle give $\mathbb E[\Delta\theta]\simeq b\Delta t$ and $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)\simeq2D\Delta t$. Correlated perturbations, preferred states, or boundaries can invalidate that short-lag fit. At long delays, report the distribution of angular errors around the circle. Values separated by a full turn represent the same angle, so a local unwrapped variance cannot be extended indefinitely as a measure of angular error.

Estimate readout noise before interpreting short-lag variance as motion of the stored value. Independent errors with constant variance in two position readings add a constant offset to the measured displacement variance.

Suppose each position estimate contains independent, zero-mean measurement error with variance $\sigma_m^2$. The difference of two estimates then adds $2\sigma_m^2$ to displacement variance, even when the circuit does not move. For independent constant-$D$ state motion, the measured short-lag displacement variance is $2D\Delta t+2\sigma_m^2$. A nonzero intercept can reveal this contribution. Correlated readout errors, overlapping observation windows, or a state that changes during the readout require a fuller model. This is the same type of separation needed when interpreting the eye-drift measurements.

A changed component affects memory through the circuit's equations. Increasing a leak current can shorten a component time constant. Changing a recurrent weight can alter restoration or introduce a preferred angle. A fluctuating current can perturb many neurons, yet only part of the resulting activity change remains as a change of the remembered angle.

The [projection derived in Part I](ch-memory-dynamics.html#sec-memory-linearization) makes the last statement precise. Let the vector $\mathbf r$ contain the network's activity variables, with local dynamics $d\mathbf r=\mathbf f(\mathbf r)dt+B\,d\mathbf W_t$. The matrix $B$ maps independent Brownian disturbances into those variables. Near a family $\mathbf r_*(\theta)$ of steady states, let $\boldsymbol\ell$ be the left neutral vector, normalized so that $\boldsymbol\ell^T d\mathbf r_*/d\theta=1$. It converts an activity disturbance into its surviving angular displacement. The leading local approximation gives

[Noise matters through both its size and the directions in which it pushes the circuit.]{.key-statement} Large disturbances in rapidly corrected directions can matter less than small disturbances along the memory direction. In a general network the left neutral vector differs from the visible tangent to the family. Using the tangent alone can predict the wrong sensitivity. Curvature and state-dependent noise can also contribute drift beyond this local approximation.

Write $\delta\theta\simeq\boldsymbol\ell^T\delta\mathbf r$ in the local linear regime. For the neutral mode, $\boldsymbol\ell^T$ times the linearized deterministic drift is zero. The stochastic increment is $d\theta\simeq\boldsymbol\ell^TB\,d\mathbf W_t$. Since $\operatorname{Cov}(d\mathbf W_t)=I\,dt$, its variance is $\boldsymbol\ell^TBB^T\boldsymbol\ell\,dt$. Equating this to $2D\,dt$ gives the displayed coefficient. The normalization ensures that the result measures angular displacement rather than an arbitrarily scaled activity coordinate. This calculation transfers only after the hardware's local dynamics and noise assumptions have been checked.

**Example: a tighter distribution can hide a biased memory.**

Consider two illustrative circuits after a one-second delay. Circuit A has zero mean angular error and variance $4$ deg$^2$. Circuit B has mean error $3^\circ$ and variance $1$ deg$^2$, because it is attracted toward a preferred angle. Their mean squared errors are $4$ and $1+3^2=10$ deg$^2$. Circuit B has less random spread but worse cue retention. Reporting only its smaller variance would hide the effect of pinning.
The source papers supply different constraints on this hardware experiment.

**Burak and Fiete (2012):** compare diffusion with the information available in spikes under matched noise, dynamics, and observation assumptions. A processor that stores an exact internal angle and exposes it directly to the decoder has changed the readout problem.

**Ben-Shushan and colleagues (2022):** a measured output can filter the internal command. Camera exposure, output smoothing, or a mechanical actuator can change the observed motion. Calibrate that path before assigning an output time scale to the memory circuit itself.

These links concern the tested mechanisms, not a claim that a chip reproduces the animal systems. The [synthesis chapter](ch-synthesis.html#sec-synthesis-evidence) sets out the evidence supplied by the original papers.

Time conversion is especially important for accelerated hardware. If model time $t_m=a t_p$, where $t_p$ is physical time and $a>1$ is the acceleration factor, a diffusion law $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)=2D_m t_m$ becomes $2(aD_m)t_p$. The result is $D_p=aD_m$ when expressed per physical second. This is a change of units for the same ideal trajectory. Physical communication delay, temperature drift, or limited readout speed can prevent a real device from obeying that ideal rescaling.

For an energy comparison, specify the cue distribution, delay, permitted decoding error, and failed-trial rate. Measure energy over writing, waiting, and reading, including required host processing and interfaces. Then report how error and energy change as delay increases. An operations-per-second or operations-per-watt figure alone cannot establish the cost of retaining a useful value.

The resulting research question is concrete: **which part of the physical implementation limits the accuracy of a remembered quantity, and does changing that part improve retention under the same task and readout?** That question turns von Neumann's comparison into a test of contemporary neural and electronic memory mechanisms.

Burak and Fiete (2012) derive memory diffusion from assumptions about recurrent connections and random spike timing. To test that prediction, they simulate individual spikes and measure how the stored value moves. The central result remains an analytical bound. The simulations check its predicted motion in different network designs, including the limits imposed by an angular coordinate.

The physical idea is continuing neural activity after a cue has ended. A spike briefly increases synaptic activation. That activation decays, but it also changes the rates at which other neurons fire. Recurrent connections can therefore renew the activity. Random event times disturb the pattern that represents the remembered value.
The computer stores each neuron's synaptic activation $s_i$. The recurrent input $g_i$ and firing rate $r_i$ are calculated from it:

Here $W_{ij}$ is the connection from neuron $j$ to neuron $i$, $b_i$ is a constant input, and $\phi$ converts total input into a rate in spikes per second. In the paper's normalization, each spike increases $s_i$ by one and activation decays with time constant $\tau$. The [earlier neural mechanism and derivation](ch-foundations.html#sec-memory-spikes) explain these variables and the continuous-time equations.[^simmem-model]
One short simulation step has a causal order:
Read the current activations and calculate the recurrent inputs and firing rates.
Generate spikes using those rates and the chosen time interval.
Apply synaptic decay and the increments caused by those spikes.
Decode the represented value and repeat after the external cue is absent.

The ring simulation uses an [[**Euler update**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, which approximates a variable's change over a short interval by its current derivative times that interval.]{.definition-explanation} For decay alone, an interval $h$ changes $s_i$ to approximately $s_i(1-h/\tau)$. Spike increments are added according to the event model. This finite step approximates the continuous dynamics, so its accuracy must be checked at the resolution needed for the reported statistic.

[Each generated spike changes the recurrent inputs and can change the rates of later spikes.]{.key-statement} The theory explains when these interacting changes can be described by diffusion of one coordinate.

In the ring model, neurons are ordered by their preferred angles. Their connections support a localized activity pattern whose position represents an angle. Figure 2A–D compares the wandering position with predictions calculated from the network's steady tuning curves. Two transfer functions test different relationships between diffusion and spike information: the exponential case attains the bound under the model assumptions, while the illustrated sigmoid case lies above it.[^simmem-ring]

The comparison separates prediction from measurement. First, solve the noise-free network for its steady activity pattern and calculate the predicted diffusion coefficient and information rate. Then run the stochastic network and measure its angular displacement. For this simulation the authors decode the angle of the neuron with the largest instantaneous rate. That convenient numerical readout differs from the ideal spike-based estimator studied later in the paper.

At short lags, the displacement variance tests the local relation $\operatorname{Var}(\Delta\theta)\simeq2D\ell$, where $D$ has units of angle squared per second and $\ell$ is the lag in seconds. At long lags, the reported differences are wrapped into $(-\pi,\pi)$, so the mean square levels off. The long-lag comparison uses a diffusion calculation with periodic boundaries. This saturation limits the reported angular error. It does not recover the initial angle.

The Methods specify 1,024 neurons, synaptic time constant 10 ms, and update interval 0.1 ms. Each step generates a spike with probability $r_i h$. This one-event approximation requires that probability to remain small. There are 100 trials of 1,000 seconds each. The displacement analysis excludes the first 10 ms. Error bars are standard errors across trials.
Writing $\alpha$ for the separation of preferred angles, the finite network uses

The common input is $b=-2$. The two transfer rules are $\tau\phi(g)=10e^g$ and $\tau\phi(g)=0.2[1+\tanh(g+4)]$. Initial activations are independently uniform between 0 and 0.01. These settings describe the finite simulation. The supporting text separately divides a connection rule by $N$ to study larger populations. Applying that extra factor here would change the reported weights.

The symmetric-network prediction uses the squared input slope in its numerator. Burak and Fiete's 2017 correction confirms that square, which was missing in the supplied Early Edition's Eq. 2. The correction does not change these simulation settings.[^simmem-correction]

A second network contains two mutually inhibiting units, interpreted also as two neural populations. Increasing one population's activity while decreasing the other's changes the stored value. Figure 2E–G tests diffusion in this family without relying on rotational symmetry. The diffusion calculation applies to both models because each has a continuous family of states and restoring dynamics toward that family.[^simmem-two]

The Methods report cross-couplings of $-1$, no self-coupling, common input $b=5{,}000$, time constant 100 ms, update interval 0.4 ms, and duration 200 seconds. The transfer rule is $\tau r_i=g_i$ in the valid positive-rate range. These large rates can represent aggregate population activity. They should not be read as ordinary firing rates of two biological cells.

Converting between activation and rate changes the units of the stored value. Let $\theta_s=s_1-s_2$ be the activation difference and $\theta_r=r_1-r_2$ the rate difference along the steady-state family. Since $s_i=\tau r_i$ there, $\theta_r=\theta_s/\tau$ and their diffusion coefficients satisfy $D_r=D_s/\tau^2$. Their units differ, so their numerical values should not be compared without this conversion. A population can also emit several spikes within one update. The ring's at-most-one-spike rule cannot be copied into this setting. The paper specifies a Poisson process but does not say how spike counts were drawn or give the complete initial state for this example.

The supporting text also tests a mutually excitatory pair in Figure S1. Across 4,000 trials started at the same coordinate, its variance grows linearly even though the local diffusion coefficient depends on the state. The guide's [long-delay chapter](ch-memory-long-delays.html#sec-memory-long-time) explains the coordinate and the printed factor-of-two discrepancy. That discrepancy is separate from the authors' 2017 correction.

Figures 3 and S2 plot formulas for readout error. They compare an ideal estimator with an estimator that weights all observations equally as the observation interval grows. The sources do not describe an additional spiking-network experiment or a biological circuit implementing ideal estimation in these figures.

The paper specifies its network equations and several numerical settings, but does not identify a programming language or simulator package. No public simulation-code archive was identified in the checked paper, supplement, or author publication entries. This describes the search as of October 30, 2026. It is not proof that no code exists. A new implementation must document choices the paper leaves open, including how it generates random numbers and events for aggregate populations.

[The simulations show that the stated network models can produce the predicted memory errors. Connecting those errors to animal behavior requires a measurement model and biological data.]{.key-statement} Ben-Shushan et al. (2022) add those elements by following an internal eye-position command through motor neurons and muscles to measured motion.

Ben-Shushan et al. (2022) ask whether fluctuations in a neural memory circuit can explain the small eye movements that continue during fixation. Their simulation must turn a changing neural command into muscle action and eye position. It must also produce signals that can be analyzed like the recordings. The paper's central evidence combines a shared-source inference from data with a model showing that a noisy integrator can account for the observed motion.

The empirical analysis uses earlier recordings of 57 ocular motor neurons from two macaques, paired with eye-position measurements. These are separate single-cell recordings, not a simultaneous recording of all 57 neurons. The authors fit each cell's relation to eye position, velocity, and acceleration, then use it to reconstruct movement from that cell's spikes. A trial held out of the fit tests prediction on data that did not determine the fitted parameters.[^simeye-data]

After excluding rapid eye movements, the analysis compares measured and reconstructed displacements over 350 ms segments. Their covariance supports a substantial shared drive upstream of the motor neurons. The estimate near 82% depends on calibrated gains and the assumed separation of shared and private fluctuations. It is not a measurement of noise inside the integrator itself.

The authors then test whether an integrator with plausible cellular properties can generate enough shared motion, with the right timing, after the motor pathway filters it. Its tuning distributions and spike variability are constrained by earlier physiological studies. Some remaining choices are adjusted to compare with the measured drift. The paper notes that several parameter combinations can match its magnitude.
The model has four connected stages. Each stage changes a different physical or represented quantity:

**Integrator activity:** two opposing neural populations sustain a represented eye-position command. Spikes renew decaying synaptic activity, and recurrent input sets later firing rates. A weighted difference between the populations produces the command $E_{\mathrm{OI}}$.

**Motor-neuron spikes:** each simulated motor neuron receives that command. Its tuning slope and threshold convert the commanded angle into a firing rate. Spike generation adds that neuron's private variability.
**Muscle and eye response:** filtered motor activity drives a mechanical response with position, velocity, and acceleration terms. Combining the motor contributions gives the eye angle $E$.

**Delayed visual feedback:** the difference between an earlier eye position and the current internal command changes the integrator's input. The delay prevents this correction from acting instantaneously.[^simeye-model]

[The internal command and the physical eye angle are separate outputs. The muscles smooth rapid command fluctuations, so the eye's short-lag motion need not have the same statistics as the neural state.]{.key-statement} The [eye-timing chapter](ch-eye-timing.html) derives a simplified filtering example. The [circuit chapter](ch-eye-circuit.html) explains the full model's neural assumptions.

The circuit structure is adapted from Aksay et al. (2007), with tuning and noise assumptions adjusted to primate evidence. Its weights are fitted so that a range of commands can persist in the mean-rate model. This is different from fitting an eye-drift trace.

The spikes are more regular than a Poisson process. The model generates candidate events at $M$ times the desired rate and retains every $M$th event. At constant rate, each retained interval sums $M$ exponential waiting times, giving interval coefficient of variation $1/\sqrt M$. This preserves the mean firing rate while reducing interval variability. The published simulations use integrator variability around 0.22 and motor-neuron variability around 0.07.

Simulated spike times are drawn by a program that generates a repeatable sequence of random-looking numbers. A [[**random seed**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} sets its starting state, allowing the same implementation and sequence of calls to reproduce those samples.]{.definition-explanation} The spike-generation rule specifies the intended distribution; the seed chooses the sample sequence.

The final main Methods report an integrator size $N=30{,}000$, 1,000 motor neurons, synaptic time constant 20 ms, and feedback strength $A=0.015$. The feedback delay is about 70 ms. These are the main model settings, not values to combine with the different comparison runs in the supplement.

The inspected MATLAB code sets its internal update interval to $10^{-5}$ s and saves every 100 steps, giving 1 ms output samples. It uses a 10 ms motor-neuron synaptic time constant, initializes central gaze, and sets the random seed from the trajectory index. Synaptic decay is updated by first-order Euler steps. The mechanical calculation updates velocity and then position.

The code's `N` creates a vector in each of the paired populations, whereas the paper describes $N$ as the network's neuron number. That convention must be resolved before claiming a function call reproduces the published size. The code also uses a different motor-neuron variability regression from the final printed Eq. 35.[^simeye-code]
One matching trajectory is weak evidence because many mechanisms can look irregular. The paper compares outputs after changing sources of variability or feedback:

**Private motor noise alone:** with a constant central command, independent motor-neuron fluctuations produce limited, saturating displacement variance. Figure 3 compares this contribution with the larger continued drift in the recordings.

**Noisy integrator before the muscles:** Figure 4 measures the simulated internal command. At sufficiently long lags, its mean squared displacement approaches the linear dependence expected for diffusion.
**Full pathway:** Figure 5 compares the final eye output with the recordings. Muscle filtering shapes the short-lag behavior, while delayed feedback changes the longer-lag behavior.

**Measurement procedure applied to simulated signals:** simulated motor spikes and eye motion are passed through the same reconstruction and covariance analysis used for the recordings. This tests whether the analysis can recover the shared contribution under a model where its origin is known.[^simeye-figures]

The supplement adds checks of measurement-noise subtraction, feedback removal, and the contribution of direct output spiking noise. In the last check, noise still drives the internal integrator, so removing motor-output noise does not turn the entire model deterministic.

These controls support the integrator as a sufficient explanation under the tested assumptions. They do not show that it is the only central circuit capable of producing the recordings. The shared-source estimate from data and the proposed location of that source remain different conclusions.

The authors release MATLAB `.m` functions and `.mat` parameter files. `Run_model.m` starts trajectories and their mean-squared-displacement analysis. `Full_model_simulation.m` updates the integrator, motor neurons, and eye. `Fit_OI_circuit.m` fits a persistent mean-rate circuit, while the analysis routines compare generated trajectories with an already processed empirical MSD file.[^simeye-code]

The separately deposited raw recordings contain one spreadsheet per cell and one sheet per trial. The columns give horizontal and vertical eye angles and spike times. Eye samples are spaced by 1 ms. Reanalyzing those recordings tests the empirical reconstruction. Running the model tests a proposed source of the motion. Loading the processed MSD file alone does not reproduce the raw-data analysis.[^simeye-deposit]

The inspected repository does not specify a MATLAB version or a complete environment. Source calls include constrained least squares, random sampling, and correlation routines, whose required functions and toolboxes must be available. The repository's `rate` branch calls a function absent from the inspected file tree. These are practical limits to check before treating the package as a complete figure-reproduction workflow. No such end-to-end run is claimed here.

For a neurophysics study, the useful next calculation is controlled: vary one cellular or mechanical assumption, keep the measurement procedure fixed, and examine which observed statistic changes. Mainali et al. (2025) use a different form of this reasoning. Their simulations change spatial maps and measure the regions where cells would fire, without simulating eye motion or a time-dependent memory circuit.

Mainali et al. (2025) ask whether one statistical model can explain the many firing regions observed in hippocampal place cells across different environments. Their simulation generates a cell's firing-rate map over space and measures the active regions. Position is the independent variable. The generated map is fixed while it is analyzed, so this simulation addresses spatial coding rather than how a neural circuit retains a position over time.

For each model cell, the theory assigns a smooth Gaussian input field $h(\mathbf x)$ to locations $\mathbf x$. Its covariance controls how similar nearby input values tend to be. A threshold determines which locations activate the cell. In the guide's notation, the rate is proportional to

Here $q$ is the dimensionless threshold, $C(0)$ is the input variance, and an overall gain converts positive excess input into a rate. The threshold and spatial correlation scale govern the shapes and sizes of the active regions. The gain supplies the firing-rate scale. The [spatial-model chapter](ch-place-fields.html) develops these quantities before deriving field-count and gap predictions.[^simplace-model]
The published Python archive constructs such maps directly:
Draw independent normally distributed values at the spatial grid points for each cell.

Smooth the array with a [[**Gaussian filter**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"}, which averages nearby values with weights that decrease with distance.]{.definition-explanation} Neighboring outputs share inputs, making them correlated.
Divide each map by the square root of the mean of its squared grid values, its root mean square. This sets its sampled root mean square to one.
Subtract the threshold and replace negative values with zero.
Measure the connected nonzero regions as fields.

This procedure implements the spatial model without explicitly simulating presynaptic neurons or their synapses. The paper's random-input argument explains one possible origin of a Gaussian field. It is not a simulated recurrent hippocampal circuit in this code. [Agreement with place-field statistics tests the spatial description, while the proposed wiring remains an interpretation requiring further evidence.]{.key-statement}
Smoothing, amplitude normalization, and edge handling affect the finite sampled map. Matching the published implementation requires these numerical choices.[^simplace-code]

The authors choose threshold and spatial scale to match a small number of measured summaries. For the long 200 m bat tunnel, they match mean field length and mean gap. In the short 6 m tunnel, they use mean field length and occupied fraction, because many cells have only one field. The 2D comparison fits mean field size and count, while the 3D comparison uses mean volume and occupied fraction.[^simplace-fit]

A [[**fitted statistic**]{.definition-term custom-style="Definition Term"} is a measured summary used to choose a model's parameters.]{.definition-explanation} Recovering that statistic checks the fit, but gives less independent evidence than successfully describing other features. The full size distribution, lower-dimensional slices, multiple peaks, and holes in fields provide further comparisons. Some of those analyses also fit a firing-rate gain, which must remain visible when judging how independent a test is.

The paper compares simulated size distributions with a fitted lognormal alternative using likelihood-based criteria. This is a comparison on the available data, rather than a reported test on a separate held-out dataset. Its high-threshold analytical laws also have a different role from finite-threshold simulation: the simulations can examine regimes where those limiting formulas are only approximate.

For uncertainty in size histograms, the Methods describe $10^4$ model realizations, each containing the experimental number of cells. The resulting spread reflects variation between model samples of that size. It does not include every source of recording error or uncertainty about the biological model.

To compare a generated field with a recorded one, both must be measured in compatible ways. A small positive noise value can connect two regions, while thresholding can split them. Smoothing can remove a peak or fill a small hole.
The STAR Methods specify several distinct measurements:
**Lengths and gaps in 1D:** count consecutive nonzero or zero bins and convert their counts to physical lengths. The archived implementation places field edges at grid-bin boundaries.

**Volumes in 3D:** label connected nonzero components and multiply their bin counts by bin volume. The reported analysis removes fields more than three standard deviations above the mean volume as probable mergers.
**Peak and boundary shape:** use peak detection and local finite differences, with additional smoothing or rate thresholds stated for the relevant comparison.

**Connectedness and holes:** use the Gudhi Python library to calculate Betti numbers and form their alternating sum, the Euler characteristic. The [place-field tests chapter](ch-place-tests.html) explains why this statistic contains information absent from field volumes alone.[^simplace-measure]

The experimental 3D maps have 10 cm spatial bins and receive a median filter in the described processing. Different analyses use different cutoffs. A reproduction therefore needs the rule for its target panel, rather than one generic threshold applied to every figure.

Figures 1 and 2 connect the generated maps to size, count, gap, and slice statistics. Figure 3 tests shapes and connectedness. Figures 4 and 5 examine how fitted parameters and threshold changes relate to field structure. The supplement checks alternative spherical fields, cell-to-cell threshold variation, and sensitivity to processing choices. These comparisons extend the evidence beyond a visually similar random map.

The paper defines its local correlation scale by $\ell=\sqrt{-C(0)/C''(0)}$ in one dimension. The code also uses a parameter called `sigma`, but as the width $b$ of the Gaussian smoothing filter. For ideal continuous white noise smoothed by a Gaussian of width $b$, the covariance is proportional to $\exp[-x^2/(4b^2)]$. Differentiating at zero gives $\ell=\sqrt2\,b$. The two widths are therefore different quantities.

This conversion follows from the smoothing construction. It is not another fitted biological result. Finite sampling and filter truncation can modify the ideal relation. The archived 1D generator uses reflected edges, whereas its 3D generator wraps the filter around the array edges. The boundary rule used for smoothing also does not, by itself, specify the boundary rule for a later topology calculation.

The README's dummy-data settings illustrate package use. They are not a complete list of the grid, cell count, and random seed used for each published panel. Exact reproduction needs those panel-specific choices as well as the archive.

The paper reports using Python 3.11. The code uses NumPy for arrays and random samples, and SciPy for smoothing and map measurements. The Methods identify SciPy routines for connected components, peak detection, and density estimation, and Gudhi for topology. These are spatial and statistical computations. A spiking-neuron simulator is not required by the released method.

The published code is archived on Zenodo, with an accompanying public GitHub repository. The inspected archive contains source files and dependency information. It does not contain all recording data or a complete set of per-figure run records. A current repository example therefore cannot automatically establish the settings used in the 2025 publication.[^simplace-code]

The article points to public source datasets, including the bat-tunnel deposit. It also acknowledges directly shared full bat maps and a 20-cell sample of rat maps used for particular analyses. Access to every required map must be checked for the intended figure. Availability of the model code is different from availability of all experimental inputs.[^simplace-data]

For a new study, two questions can now be separated. One is whether thresholded smooth random inputs describe the measured spatial patterns. The other is which neural dynamics, connections, and learning rules create those inputs. The simulations in this paper directly address the first and provide constraints for investigating the second.

A simulated eye trace can look convincing while answering the wrong question. It may use different spike statistics, a different muscle response, or a different definition of displacement from the experiment. Reproducing a result requires matching those choices before comparing curves. This chapter collects the practical decisions shared by the three papers and identifies tools for making those decisions visible.

The starting point depends on the intended result. Running the authors' program tests whether its implementation produces the reported output. Rebuilding the equations in another program tests whether an independent implementation agrees. A smaller teaching model can isolate a mechanism, but its numerical output belongs to that smaller model.

For Burak and Fiete (2012), the paper and supporting text specify the network equations and numerical settings. The inspected publication records did not identify a public simulation-code package. For Ben-Shushan et al. (2022), public MATLAB code and deposited recordings support a more direct route. Mainali et al. (2025) provide Python code and links to the source datasets. The preceding chapters identify what was checked in each package and where the inspected defaults differ from the publication.

[A successful program run establishes that the chosen program executed. Agreement with a paper also requires matching its model, parameters, measurements, and uncertainty.]{.key-statement} The simulation summaries here are source-based explanations. The guide has not rerun the authors' full simulations or reprocessed their animal recordings.

One further distinction matters for Part III. A computer can calculate a neural model, calculate a proposed transistor circuit, or collect measurements from a fabricated chip. Sun et al. (2026) report post-layout hardware simulations. Pehle et al. (2022) describe physical analog neural circuits. Both can address memory, but their outputs support different claims about an electronic device. The [hardware comparison](ch-neuromorphic-systems.html) keeps these cases separate.

The authors' implementation is the first choice when the goal is to reproduce their figures. Other libraries are useful when the goal is to isolate a mechanism or change a model. The following tools have distinct roles. The optional tools are suggestions for a new implementation, not claims about what all three papers used.
